title: The Impresario: from the World of Art to the Island of San Michele
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House of Music at Perm

stops.name: Selishchi: birth on the Volkhov
stops.date_confidence: attested; 19 March Old Style, 31 March New Style. The estate stood at the village of Selishchi on the right bank of the Volkhov, some forty-eight kilometres north of Novgorod; the coordinates are the village, not a surviving house.
stops.campa: On the family estate at Selishchi, on the right bank of the Volkhov north of Novgorod, a son is born to Pavel Pavlovich Diaghilev, a cavalry officer of a family with more name than money. The date is the nineteenth of March by the calendar Russia keeps and the thirty-first by the calendar Europe keeps, and he will live his working life on the European side of that gap. His mother dies of childbed fever within days of the birth. Within the year his father remarries, and Elena Panaeva takes the child as her own and puts music into the house around him before he can read a score.
suggested_refs: The village of Selishchi, Chudovsky district, on the Volkhov; ru.wikipedia records the 1872 birth there
sources: ru.wikipedia, 'Селищи (Чудовский район)' for the village coordinates and the birth notice

stops.name: Perm: the house on Sibirskaya Street
stops.date_confidence: the Perm years and the family salon are attested; the first romance is dated only by his age of about fifteen, which gives 1887. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The family moves east to Perm, and the house on Sibirskaya Street becomes the musical evening of the town: singers, a piano, amateur theatricals, the Urals holding a salon. This is the only conservatory the boy gets, and he is in it every evening. At about fifteen he writes a romance of his own and decides he will be a composer. The decision outlasts every proof against it. By twelve he can hold a room full of adults for a whole evening. He will never afterwards sit through a performance that is merely correct.
suggested_refs: The Diaghilev House on Sibirskaya Street, Perm, now a museum and school

segments.name: Petersburg and the World of Art

stops.name: St Petersburg Imperial University: the cousins take him in
stops.date_confidence: the arrival and matriculation in 1890 are attested and Benois dates the meeting to the summer of that year; the exact day is not recorded.
stops.campa: He comes to the capital to read law, a provincial cousin delivered into the keeping of Dmitri Filosofov's circle. Alexandre Benois and Walter Nouvel are asked to see the boy from Perm made comfortable and find a large, healthy, loud young man with an opinion on every picture in the room. The law takes him six years instead of four. The circle takes him for good: Benois, Bakst, Nouvel, Filosofov, evenings of scores and portfolios and argument, the room in which a Russian art with European manners is first talked into being.
stops.quote: I first met Diaghilev, in the summer of 1890. That year, I remained in town, and D. Filosofov, who had gone off to his estate, Bogdanovskoye, entrusted me and our common friend V. F. Nouvel, with the task of seeing that his cousin, Seriozha Diaghilev, who had just matriculated in Perm, and was about to enter the university, was made comfortable... What struck us all was his look of abounding health. He had full rosy cheeks, vermilion lips and perfect white teeth.
stops.quote_source: Alexandre Benois on their first meeting, 1890, quoted in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 27
suggested_refs: The Twelve Colleges building of St Petersburg Imperial University; Benois's memoirs of the Nevsky Pickwickians circle
sources: Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 27

stops.name: St Petersburg: the verdict on his own music
stops.date_confidence: the private lessons with Rimsky-Korsakov are attested; the year is not. Placed within the university period and defaulted to 01-01. He was never enrolled at the Conservatory.
stops.campa: He carries his own compositions to Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov and studies with him privately, never as an enrolled student of the Conservatory, where his name is on no register. The lessons end without the one thing he wants. He does not master composition to his own satisfaction, and he knows it before anybody has to tell him. He stops trying to be the man who writes the score. There is no name yet for the trade he takes up instead: deciding which score gets written, and by whom.
suggested_refs: Rimsky-Korsakov's teaching circle in St Petersburg in the 1890s

stops.name: St Petersburg: the watercolourists, a first exhibition
stops.date_confidence: the exhibition of British and German watercolourists is attested to 1897; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He brings British and German watercolourists to Petersburg and hangs them for a public that has not seen them. Nothing on the walls is his own work. He has chosen it, framed it, placed it, and talked money out of people who had not meant to give any. The show is modest and the method is already finished. He will use no other for the next thirty-two years: work the city has not seen, in the best room he can take, on one announced evening, in front of an audience with something to prove.
suggested_refs: The 1897 St Petersburg exhibition of British and German watercolours, Diaghilev's first curatorial venture

stops.name: St Petersburg: Mir iskusstva, the World of Art
stops.date_confidence: the society and the journal's first issue are attested to 1898; the month of the first number is not established in the verified pool, defaulted to 01-01. The quoted line is from the journal in 1899.
stops.campa: With Benois and the circle he founds Mir iskusstva, the World of Art, a society and a journal at once, and takes the editor's chair. He designs the pages, commissions the essays, writes criticism, and prints Russian painting beside European painting so that both are judged by one standard. Nicholas Roerich will be elected the society's president; the painters filling these pages, Bakst and Benois and Roerich, are the men who will later fill his stages in Paris.
stops.quote: One must climb the pinnacles of Florentine art to pass judgment on contemporary art.
stops.quote_source: Diaghilev in Mir Iskusstva, 1899, quoted in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 30
suggested_refs: Bound runs of Mir Iskusstva, 1898-1904, designed and edited by Diaghilev
sources: nicholas_roerich.journey.json (Roerich's presidency of the World of Art society)

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre: an officer on special duty
stops.date_confidence: the appointment by Prince Volkonsky is attested to 1899; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Prince Sergei Volkonsky, newly set over the Imperial Theatres, makes him an officer on special duty, and for two years Diaghilev works inside the machine he will spend the rest of his life outside. He sees the Mariinsky from the wings: its discipline, its ballerinas with protectors at court, its Tchaikovsky scores played as furniture, its horror of anything last season did not do. Everything he later sells to Paris he learns first in this house, including the exact list of what he means to leave behind in it.
suggested_refs: The Annual of the Imperial Theatres, redesigned by Diaghilev during his two years on the staff
sources: tchaikovsky.journey.json (the Mariinsky repertoire Diaghilev later built on)

stops.name: Mariinsky Theatre: Sylvia and the discharge
stops.date_confidence: the Sylvia commission falls in 1900 and the discharge in 1901; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01. The production was never realised.
stops.campa: He is entrusted with a new production of Delibes' Sylvia and means to make it with his own painters, in his own taste. The administration refuses, the quarrel goes public, and Volkonsky discharges him; the ballet is never staged at all. At twenty-nine he is finished in Russian officialdom. No ministry will ever again be able to cancel one of his evenings, because no ministry will ever again be paying for them, and the stage he wants is not in this country in any case.
suggested_refs: Prince Sergei Volkonsky's memoirs on the Imperial Theatres dispute of 1900-1901

stops.name: St Petersburg: Isadora Duncan dances barefoot
stops.date_confidence: placed in the weeks after Bloody Sunday, January 1905, following the atlas file; the exact evening is not established, day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Isadora Duncan dances barefoot in Petersburg in the weeks when the city is still burying the dead of Bloody Sunday, and Diaghilev is in the house with Fokine, Pavlova, and Kschessinska. He does not want the technique. What he takes is the permission inside it: a body can be moved by a score instead of by a syllabus, and a Russian audience will sit still for it. Fokine leaves the theatre already loosening the classical grammar he was raised inside, and four years later Diaghilev takes Fokine, and that loosened grammar, to Paris.
suggested_refs: Kschessinska's memoir on the impression Duncan's Petersburg performances made on Fokine

stops.name: Tauride Palace: four thousand Russian faces
stops.date_confidence: attested to 6 March 1905; the scale of more than four thousand portraits is given by the same source.
stops.campa: In the halls of the Tauride Palace he hangs more than four thousand Russian historical portraits, gathered by travelling to the country houses himself and talking families out of their ancestors. It is the largest thing of its kind attempted in Russia, and it is an inventory of a class taken in the year that class begins to end. Many of these canvases will burn in the revolutions to come, and this remains the last occasion on which most of them stand in one room. He assembles them while assembling is still possible, and then he leaves.
suggested_refs: The 1905 Tauride Palace exhibition of Russian historical portraiture, catalogued by Diaghilev
sources: OpenStreetMap for the Tauride Palace, Shpalernaya 47

stops.name: Grand Palais: two centuries of Russian art
stops.date_confidence: the Salon d'Automne exhibition is attested to October 1906; the opening day is not established, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes Russia west. At the Salon d'Automne in the Grand Palais he mounts two centuries of Russian art, some seven hundred and fifty works, icons through Vrubel and Bakst, for a city that has been importing Russian novels and sending nothing back. The Russian rooms are the event of the season. What pays in Paris, he learns here, is Russia hung with Parisian tact in the best room the city will let him have. The paintings go home afterwards. He does not.
suggested_refs: The 1906 Salon d'Automne Russian section at the Grand Palais, hung by Diaghilev and Bakst

stops.name: Palais Garnier: the historic Russian concerts
stops.date_confidence: the Concerts historiques russes are attested to May 1907; individual concert dates are not established in the verified pool, day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Pictures are followed by sound. Diaghilev fills a series of concerts at the Opera with Russian music, Rimsky-Korsakov conducting his own scores, Chaliapin singing, and an audience that came out of curiosity staying out of appetite. Each season he raises the stake, and each season he pays for it by charming subscriptions out of Parisian hostesses and Petersburg grand dukes in the same week. He will still be raising it twenty years later, and still paying for it in the same week.
suggested_refs: The programmes of the Concerts historiques russes, Paris Opera, May 1907

stops.name: Palais Garnier: Boris Godunov and Chaliapin
stops.date_confidence: the production is attested to May 1908; the premiere day is not established in the verified pool, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He brings Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov to the Opera with Feodor Chaliapin as the Tsar. Paris has not heard singing of this kind and does not recover from it quickly. The books close on a loss of some eighty-five thousand francs. He has paid for the triumph with money he does not have, against a subscription he has not yet raised, and he answers it the following year by risking more. He is now certain that what Paris will want next, and pay more for, is dancing.
suggested_refs: The 1908 Paris Boris Godunov, with Chaliapin, staged and financed by Diaghilev

segments.name: The Saison Russe: a company out of nothing

stops.name: St Petersburg: the court withdraws its money
stops.date_confidence: the quoted grand-ducal letter to the Tsar is dated 18 March 1909; the sequence of the withdrawal of funds and of the Mariinsky's scenery is attested but not day-dated.
stops.campa: The Paris seasons run on imperial goodwill and the goodwill fails. His standing with the ballerina Mathilde Kschessinska, who has ears at court, collapses; the treasury money he had counted on is withdrawn, and with it the use of the Mariinsky's scenery and rehearsal rooms. A grand duke writes to the Tsar to warn him against the whole beastly affair and its vilest flatteries. Diaghilev loses the treasury and keeps the dancers. Out of that refusal the Ballets Russes is born private, owing nothing to a ministry and everything to a box office.
stops.quote: As was to be expected, your telegram wrought havoc in the whole Diaghilev business, and now in his attempt to save his beastly affair, he is resorting to every subterfuge, from the vilest flatteries to absolute falsehoods... We very much hope that you will not take the bait.
stops.quote_source: Letter from a Grand Duke to Tsar Nicholas II, 18 March 1909, quoted in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), pp. 132-133
suggested_refs: The 1909 court correspondence over imperial patronage of Diaghilev's Paris season

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet: the first Saison Russe
stops.date_confidence: attested: 19 May 1909, with Le Pavillon d'Armide, the Polovtsian dances from Prince Igor, and Le Festin. Les Sylphides came on the season's second programme, 2 June 1909.
stops.campa: He takes the Chatelet, has the inside of it rebuilt to his own taste, and opens on the nineteenth of May with Le Pavillon d'Armide, the Polovtsian dances out of Prince Igor in Nicholas Roerich's camp of felt and smoke, and Le Festin. Fokine has made the dances, Bakst and Benois the eye, and Karsavina, Pavlova, and Nijinsky are the bodies. Paris is converted inside a single evening, and the company that has no name yet already has a reputation the newspapers must attend to.
stops.quote: When I entered the box to which I had been invited, I arrived slightly late, not altogether believing in the revelation certain initiates had promised me; but I realized at once that something miraculous was happening, that I was witnessing something absolutely unique. Everything that could strike the imagination, intoxicate, enchant, and win one over, seemed to have been assembled on that stage, to be luxuriating there as naturally, as beautifully, as vegetation responds to a beneficent climate.
stops.quote_source: Comtesse de Noailles, writing twenty years later, quoted in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 158
suggested_refs: The programme of the first Saison Russe, Theatre du Chatelet, 19 May 1909

stops.name: Palais Garnier: The Firebird, and an unknown composer
stops.date_confidence: attested: The Firebird premiered at the Palais Garnier on 25 June 1910, not at the Chatelet; the whole 1910 season was at the Opera.
stops.campa: For the second season he needs a new Russian score, the established composers are slow, and he hands The Firebird to a young man nobody in Paris has heard of. Igor Stravinsky delivers it, and Karsavina burns through the title role at the Opera on the twenty-fifth of June. Diaghilev is still commissioning him eighteen years later. Nobody recommended this composer to him, and nobody could have: he went looking for an unknown on purpose. Scheherazade opens the same season in Bakst's greens and oranges, and Paris dressmakers are copying the costumes within the month.
suggested_refs: The autograph score of L'Oiseau de feu, commissioned by Diaghilev in 1909

stops.name: Monte Carlo: the company made permanent
stops.date_confidence: the first Monte Carlo season falls in the spring of 1911; the exact opening is not established, defaulted to 01. Monte Carlo did not become the company's formal winter base until 1922.
stops.campa: Until now each season has been gathered in the spring out of dancers on leave from the Imperial theatres. In 1911 he constitutes a permanent company, the Ballets Russes, with no home theatre, no state behind it, and no capital but his own credit, and takes its first engagement at the little Salle Garnier above the harbour at Monte Carlo. Dancers who join him now must give up their Petersburg pensions to do it. The company will not settle here as its true winter workshop for another decade, but the arrangement that ends only at his death begins on this stage.
suggested_refs: The Salle Garnier of the Opera de Monte-Carlo, the company's first and last home stage
sources: george_balanchine.journey.json:265 for the Monte Carlo pin

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet: Petrushka
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1911 at the Chatelet; the day is not established in the verified pool, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Stravinsky's second score arrives with Benois' fairground around it and Nijinsky inside the puppet's suit: a straw doll with a soul, beaten, jealous, and left twitching above the roofs after his own death. Nijinsky dances the part without a dancer's vanity, which nobody has seen a premier danseur consent to do. Diaghilev watches his lover become the finest performer in Europe and begins pushing him, that same season, toward making ballets instead of only dancing them. He pushes because a talent that repeats itself is of no further use to him.
suggested_refs: Benois's designs for Petrushka, 1911, and the Admiralty Square fairground they reconstruct

stops.name: Covent Garden: the second capital
stops.date_confidence: the London debut falls in the coronation season of June 1911; the exact opening date is not established in the verified pool.
stops.campa: The company crosses to London for the coronation of George V and gives its first English season at Covent Garden. London takes the Russians differently from Paris: less scandal, more devotion, and a subscribing public that will keep the company alive through years when Parisian enthusiasm has moved on. Diaghilev acquires the second of his two capitals. From now the year has a fixed shape, winter in Monte Carlo, spring in Paris, summer in London, and no address anywhere in it that belongs to him. He lives in hotels for the remaining eighteen years.
suggested_refs: The Royal Opera House seasons of the Ballets Russes, from the coronation summer of 1911
sources: nicholas_roerich.journey.json:183 for the Covent Garden pin

segments.name: Faun, Rite, and the Break with Nijinsky

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet: L'Apres-midi d'un faune
stops.date_confidence: attested: 29 May 1912.
stops.campa: Nijinsky's first ballet as choreographer runs twelve minutes and moves in profile, flat as a frieze around a vase, against Debussy's score. It ends with the faun lowering himself onto the nymph's dropped scarf. Half the house shouts, the Paris press divides against itself, and Diaghilev has the final gesture danced again the following night, unchanged. He has bought a season of newspapers for the price of one night's shouting. The dancer he trained has become a maker, on his terms.
suggested_refs: The Paris press controversy of May and June 1912 over the final gesture of the Faune

stops.name: Hellerau: the rhythm school outside Dresden
stops.date_confidence: the Hellerau festival is dated June 1912 and Diaghilev is named in the audience; the day is not established, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He goes to Dresden, to the garden suburb at Hellerau, where Jaques-Dalcroze has built a hall without a proscenium and drills bodies to hold a rhythm the way musicians hold it. Suzanne Perrottet is among those demonstrating; the audience runs from Shaw to Kafka to Diaghilev. Nijinsky is about to choreograph music that ordinary classical counting cannot carry, and Diaghilev has come to find whoever in this hall knows the trick of it. He leaves with the drill in his eye and a use for it already fixed.
suggested_refs: The 1912 Hellerau festival of the Jaques-Dalcroze school, and its eurhythmic method

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees: The Rite of Spring
stops.date_confidence: attested: 29 May 1913, in a theatre opened on 2 April 1913 and therefore not quite two months old. The word riot enters the record with reviews of the 1924 revival, not with the first-night notices.
stops.campa: In a theatre on the avenue Montaigne barely two months open, Stravinsky's Rite of Spring goes up with Roerich's designs and Nijinsky's stamping, turned-in choreography, and the audience fights itself. Catcalls drown the orchestra. Diaghilev has the house lights flicked on and off to shame the room quiet, and the performance is played to the end. The reviews of the night are mixed rather than horrified; the legend of the riot hardens later, around the revival of 1924. What he wanted has happened regardless: the music cannot be ignored.
suggested_refs: First-night notices of Le Sacre du printemps, 29 May 1913, compared with the 1924 revival reviews
sources: coco_chanel.journey.json / gurdjieff.journey.json for the Champs-Elysees pin

stops.name: Venice: the season he does not sail
stops.date_confidence: the company sailed for South America in August 1913 without him and he stayed in Venice; the day is not established, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The company sails for South America in August and he does not sail with it. He says he has been warned that he will die on the water. Those who know him best suggest another reason, that he wants a season out of Nijinsky's company. He spends the weeks in Venice instead, the city he comes back to every year the way other men come back to a family house. For the first time in five years Nijinsky crosses an ocean without Diaghilev deciding what he eats, wears, reads, and dances. Romola de Pulszky is aboard, and has waited a year and a half for exactly this.
suggested_refs: The 1913 South American tour of the Ballets Russes, made without its director

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Nijinsky marries in port
stops.date_confidence: attested: 10 September 1913, in port at Buenos Aires. Whether the ceremony was civil or religious is not established. The proposal at sea days earlier is attested.
stops.campa: The company reaches Buenos Aires and Nijinsky marries Romola de Pulszky in port on the tenth of September, days after proposing to her at sea. The world's press has the news before Diaghilev does. Later on the tour Nijinsky misses a performance in Rio while his wife is ill, and that missed performance will serve as the paper reason for what follows. Diaghilev learns of the marriage in Europe from Vassili, the servant he had sent out with the company, and is reported weeping in Russian despair and going on a wild orgy of dissipation.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires marriage register of 10 September 1913, and the world press reports of it
sources: victoria_ocampo.journey.json for the canonical Buenos Aires pin

stops.name: Paris: the telegram
stops.date_confidence: the dismissal follows the marriage in the autumn of 1913; Lifar places the telegram as reaching Nijinsky when the company was about to start back from America. Month and day are reconstruction, defaulted to 10-01.
stops.campa: He answers with two sentences in French, wired to a dancer about to start home across the ocean. There is no appeal and no meeting, and the two men never discuss it again. The man who made Nijinsky the legend of Europe removes him from the company by telegram and has Fokine back at work within weeks. Nijinsky tries to found a company of his own in London and it collapses inside a month. He has ended the career he built, and he goes on to build the next one on identical terms, and the one after that.
stops.quote: Le Ballet Russe n'a plus besoin de vos services. Ne nous rejoignez pas. Serge de Diaghilev.
stops.quote_source: Telegram from Diaghilev to Nijinsky, 1913, quoted in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 148
suggested_refs: The dismissal telegram of 1913, reproduced in Lifar's biography

segments.name: The War Years: no country, no theatre

stops.name: Ouchy: the company scattered, the next one begun
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the biographical tradition (Buckle, Diaghilev, 1979): a Swiss base in 1914-1915. Month and day are not established, defaulted to 09-01.
stops.campa: War closes the theatres and scatters the dancers across Europe, interned or conscripted where they stand. Diaghilev settles for a season in neutral Switzerland above the lake, with what remains of his people within reach and a young man he took up in Moscow, Leonide Massine, whom he is teaching to be a choreographer out of nothing: painting by painting, church by church, book by book. He has no theatre and no country, and nothing is coming in. He builds the next repertory anyway, in a rented house, for an audience that does not exist.
suggested_refs: Richard Buckle, Diaghilev (1979), on the Swiss and Italian war years
sources: Richard Buckle, Diaghilev (1979), via the general biographical tradition

stops.name: Teatro Real, Madrid: a king for a patron
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish seasons and the patronage of Alfonso XIII are attested to the war years, roughly 1916-1918; no single date, defaulted to 1916-01-01.
stops.campa: Spain is neutral and Alfonso XIII is curious. The king becomes patron of a company that is stranded and nearly broke, attends its performances in Madrid, and keeps it alive on Spanish ground while Europe fights. Diaghilev, who has worked grand dukes, countesses, and American money in turn, adds a reigning king to the list without changing his manner at all. He and Massine walk the country looking at El Greco and listening to cante jondo, and the Spain the company will later put on stage begins here as survival rather than taste.
suggested_refs: The wartime Madrid seasons of the Ballets Russes under the patronage of Alfonso XIII

stops.name: New York: the crossing he said he would not make
stops.date_confidence: the first American tour opened at the Century Theatre in January 1916; the Metropolitan Opera House engagement falls in April, and Nijinsky reached New York on 4 April 1916. The coordinates are the old Met at 1411 Broadway.
stops.campa: The company tours America, opening at the Century Theatre in January and reaching the Metropolitan Opera House in the spring, and Diaghilev crosses the Atlantic himself, everything he has said about dying at sea notwithstanding. Nijinsky, interned in Hungary since 1914 as an enemy subject, is freed in a negotiation reported to have reached the Pope and President Wilson, and lands in New York on the fourth of April to dance for the company again. The two men work at arm's length, courteously, and never repair what was broken.
stops.quote: I do not regret my relations with Serge Pavlovitch, whatever morality may say.
stops.quote_source: Vaslav Nijinsky to his wife, c. 1914, quoted via Romola Nijinsky in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 148
suggested_refs: The 1916 American tour contracts, and the prisoner exchange that released Nijinsky

stops.name: Teatro Costanzi, Rome: four men locked in a room
stops.date_confidence: the Rome rehearsal period with Picasso, Cocteau, and Massine is attested to 1917; the month is not established, defaulted to 02-01.
stops.campa: The company works in Rome through the winter, in a city loud with Futurists, while Parade is assembled: Cocteau's scenario, Picasso's cubist costumes, Massine's choreography, and a score by Erik Satie, whom Cocteau has fetched out of Arcueil for the purpose. He shuts four men who would never otherwise share a room into one, and refuses to let them out until there is a ballet. Picasso enters the theatre through this door and does not leave it for years. Massine, a boy three years ago, is making the most advanced work in Europe.
suggested_refs: The Rome studios and rehearsals of early 1917 where Parade was assembled
sources: OpenStreetMap for the Teatro Costanzi, now Teatro dell'Opera di Roma

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet: Parade
stops.date_confidence: attested: 18 May 1917, Theatre du Chatelet.
stops.campa: Parade opens in the third year of the war: a typewriter and a siren in the pit, a horse built out of two men, managers walking about as cubist buildings, and Satie's music flatly refusing to swell. The house is hostile. Apollinaire, writing the programme note, reaches for the word surrealisme and gives the century a term it keeps. Diaghilev has moved the company off Russian folklore for good. From here the Ballets Russes is a French modernist enterprise danced by Russian exiles, and its painters are the painters of Paris.
suggested_refs: Apollinaire's programme note for Parade, 18 May 1917, source of the word surrealisme

stops.name: Paris: the country behind him closes
stops.date_confidence: the October Revolution is dated 7 November 1917 New Style; Diaghilev's permanent severance from Russia is attested to 1917 as a consequence, not to a single day.
stops.campa: The revolution takes Petersburg, and with it the school, the pensions, the ballerinas in reserve, and the private money that has underwritten twenty years of his work. He is forty-five and permanently abroad. The dancers standing in his rehearsal room become exiles on the day the news arrives, and the ones who stayed behind are lost to him. He never goes back and never asks to. Whatever of Russia he exported is now only what is in this room, and he has twelve years left to turn it into something that does not need Russia at all.
suggested_refs: Soviet criticism of Diaghilev as bourgeois decadence, and his omission from Russian art history for sixty years

segments.name: The Paris Company: couturiers and cubists

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees: the dressmaker pays
stops.date_confidence: the revival of Le Sacre du printemps and Chanel's secret underwriting are attested to 1920; the December placing follows the revival's Paris performances and the exact date is not established.
stops.campa: He revives The Rite of Spring with new choreography by Massine, and the money for it comes from a dressmaker. Gabrielle Chanel gives it on the one condition that nobody is told, and he takes it and tells nobody. In the spring he introduced her to Stravinsky; by September the composer, his wife, and their four children are living in her villa at Garches. Courts and grand dukes have stopped paying for the company. Couturiers and department-store heirs pay for it now, and Diaghilev has followed the money without appearing to look at it.
suggested_refs: The 1920 revival of Le Sacre du printemps, and Chanel's undisclosed subvention of it

stops.name: Alhambra Theatre, London: The Sleeping Princess
stops.date_confidence: the London production is attested to 1921; the opening night is not established in the verified pool, day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He mounts Tchaikovsky's Sleeping Beauty in London under the title The Sleeping Princess, in Bakst's designs, at a scale nobody has attempted outside Petersburg: full length, full orchestra, the old classical text restored instead of replaced. It is his one act of piety, an offering to the theatre that discharged him twenty years earlier. London does not come. The run goes on losing money until the scenery is impounded against the debt, and the company that survived a world war is nearly finished by a nineteenth-century ballet.
suggested_refs: Bakst's designs for The Sleeping Princess, 1921, and the impounding of the sets against the company's debt

stops.name: Monte Carlo: a winter home at last
stops.date_confidence: Monte Carlo becomes the formal winter home and rehearsal base from 1922; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Ruined in London, he accepts what he has avoided for thirteen years and takes a permanent winter base. From now the company rehearses at the Salle Garnier above the harbour, engaged by the principality, and every new work is built here before it is shown in Paris or London. Diaghilev keeps hotel rooms and lives out of trunks, as he has since 1911. He is fifty, diabetic, refuses examination, eats what he pleases, and runs dancers, composers, and painters from a chair at the side of the rehearsal floor, in a hat and an overcoat.
suggested_refs: The Monte Carlo engagement of the Ballets Russes, 1922-1929, and its rehearsal seasons at the Salle Garnier

stops.name: Theatre de la Gaite-Lyrique: Les Noces
stops.date_confidence: attested: 13 June 1923.
stops.campa: Bronislava Nijinska, Nijinsky's sister, gives him Les Noces: Stravinsky's peasant wedding for four pianos, percussion, and chorus, danced by a company in plain brown and white, massed and hammering, with no ornament anywhere in it. It is the harshest work the Ballets Russes has shown, and Diaghilev counts it among the most important things he has done. Russia appears in it as ritual instead of colour, made by people who cannot go home, ten years after the painted fairground of Petrushka and a whole world away from it.
suggested_refs: Nijinska's choreography for Les Noces, 1923, and Goncharova's designs for it

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees: Le Train Bleu
stops.date_confidence: attested: 20 June 1924, in Paris at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees, not in Monte Carlo as the ballet's Riviera subject often suggests.
stops.campa: Cocteau writes a beach: acrobats, golfers, a tennis champion, bathing costumes by Gabrielle Chanel, a curtain enlarged from a Picasso gouache, choreography by Nijinska. The Ballets Russes is now dressing the season it is satirising, and the woman whose clothes are on the stage is quietly paying part of the bill for the evening. Diaghilev, who arrived in Paris fifteen years ago with icons and Chaliapin, is selling the Riviera back to the people who invented it, and getting there before they do.
suggested_refs: Picasso's curtain for Le Train Bleu and Chanel's jersey costumes, 1924

stops.name: Paris: four dancers out of Soviet Russia
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1924: Balanchine auditioned and was hired that month, not in 1925 as often stated. Day not established, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Four young dancers out of Soviet Russia, touring Germany on a permit they have no intention of honouring, audition for him in Paris. He hires them, and within months Georgi Balanchivadze, renamed Balanchine, is his ballet master and will be his last chief choreographer. Diaghilev walks him through the churches and galleries of Italy exactly as he walked Massine, teaching a choreographer how to look at things. In the same year, writing about Massine, whom he has lost, he sets down what he believes he found in him and could not keep.
stops.quote: that essential though indefinable something which made the creator in Massine... for all too short a time, alas!
stops.quote_source: Diaghilev, written 1924, quoted in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 208
suggested_refs: The November 1924 Paris audition of the Soviet State Dancers

stops.name: Venice: the notebook given to Lifar
stops.date_confidence: the inscription is signed Venice 1926; the month and day are not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. His Venetian summers are attested across the 1920s.
stops.campa: Every year he comes back to Venice, the one city he returns to with no season to sell in it, and in this one he gives Serge Lifar a notebook inscribed to the teaching of the last of the great masters, and to Venice as an eternal inspirer of all that brings peace. He signs it S. de Diaghilev, Venice 1926. Thirteen years ago he stayed in this lagoon rather than cross an ocean he had been told would kill him. A version of the line he writes here will be cut into his headstone on the island across the water.
stops.quote: I hope that these notes, drawn from the teaching of the last of the Great Masters in Venice, will remain as unforgettable and eternal as Venice itself, eternal inspirer of all that brings peace.
stops.quote_source: Diaghilev's inscription in a notebook given to Serge Lifar, signed Venice 1926, quoted in Serge Lifar, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 374
suggested_refs: The Lifar notebook of 1926, and the epitaph on the San Michele headstone that echoes it

stops.name: Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt: Apollon musagete
stops.date_confidence: attested: 12 June 1928, Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt, Paris.
stops.campa: Balanchine sets Stravinsky's Apollon musagete: three muses, a young god, a string orchestra, and almost nothing else on the stage. After twenty years of colour and ferocity the company hands Paris restraint, white tunics, and classical steps rebuilt from the inside out. Diaghilev, watching the last rehearsal, understands that the boy he hired off a German tour has made a language. It is not his own taste and he backs it anyway. Balanchine will still be building on this ballet in America forty years later.
suggested_refs: Stravinsky's score for Apollon musagete and Balanchine's 1928 choreography

stops.name: Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt: The Prodigal Son
stops.date_confidence: attested: 21 May 1929; the last ballet Diaghilev brought to the stage.
stops.campa: Prokofiev's score, Rouault's designs, Balanchine's choreography, and Lifar as the son who comes home on his knees across the stage. It is the last ballet Diaghilev brings to any stage. He is fifty-seven, ill, quarrelling with his composer over the ending, and already sizing up the young men who will carry the next ten years he assumes are coming to him. The season closes and the company disperses for the summer. He sees them off, goes to take a cure, and turns south.
suggested_refs: Rouault's designs and Prokofiev's score for Le Fils prodigue, 1929

stops.name: Vichy: the cure
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the biographical tradition (Buckle, Diaghilev, 1979): a stay at Vichy in July 1929 before travelling to Venice. Day not established, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Diabetic, swollen, unwilling to be examined properly or to give up sweets, he takes the waters at Vichy in the last weeks of July, then turns toward the Mediterranean and Venice. Boris Kochno and Serge Lifar, the two young men who have run his final decade between them, are within reach of him. He is making plans for the coming season and for new work he wants written. The doctors have told him what he has and roughly what it costs. He goes on planning through the fortnight that is left to him.
suggested_refs: Richard Buckle, Diaghilev (1979), on the last summer
sources: Richard Buckle, Diaghilev (1979), via the general biographical tradition

stops.name: Grand Hotel des Bains, Lido: the nineteenth of August
stops.date_confidence: attested: he died at the Grand Hotel des Bains on the Venice Lido on 19 August 1929, aged 57, of complications of diabetes.
stops.campa: He reaches the Lido and takes a room at the Grand Hotel des Bains, where the fever rises and the diabetes goes into its last stage. He refuses a doctor until a doctor can do nothing. On the morning of the nineteenth of August he dies in the city built on water, sixteen years after refusing to cross an ocean because he had been warned that water would take him. Kochno, Lifar, and Misia Sert are with him at the end, and Misia pays for the funeral. He is fifty-seven and owns almost nothing at all.
suggested_refs: The Grand Hotel des Bains, Lungomare Marconi 17, Venice Lido

stops.name: Isola di San Michele: the Orthodox ground
stops.date_confidence: the burial in the Orthodox section of San Michele is attested; the interment date of 21 August is traditional rather than documented.
stops.campa: The coffin crosses the lagoon by gondola and is carried up onto the island on the arms of the men who worked for him. He is buried in the Orthodox ground, among Russians who died out of Russia. The stone takes the Venice line from the notebook he inscribed three years earlier. Dancers leave their shoes on it for decades afterwards. In Paris the company, twenty years old, carrying its debts and holding no one able to replace him, dissolves within months of the funeral, and its people scatter into every ballet company of the century.
stops.quote: the body was wafted to the island of San Michele, and there borne on our arms to the grave
stops.quote_source: Serge Lifar, eyewitness to the funeral, Serge Diaghilev: His Life, His Work, His Legend (1940), p. 373
suggested_refs: The Orthodox enclosure of the Cimitero di San Michele, Venice, and Diaghilev's headstone

stops.name: Isola di San Michele: Stravinsky comes to the same island
stops.date_confidence: attested: Stravinsky died 6 April 1971 and was buried on San Michele on 15 April 1971; Vera de Bosset was buried there in 1982.
stops.campa: Forty-two years later Igor Stravinsky, who came to him at twenty-seven unknown and left him the composer of the century, is brought to the same island by his own wish and buried a few paces off; Vera de Bosset joins him in 1982. The Firebird, Petrushka, The Rite of Spring, Les Noces, Apollon: the whole line of scores that made the Ballets Russes worth arguing about lies here beside the man who commissioned every one of them. Around them, in the Orthodox enclosure, the Russians of the emigration. None of them went home.
suggested_refs: The graves of Stravinsky and Vera de Bosset in the Orthodox enclosure of San Michele
